issues.legal_issue: A buyer seeking specific performance must prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential contractual obligations, assessed from financial capacity and conduct.
material_facts: The agreement required the buyer to pay the balance consideration within six months and required the sellers, upon receiving it, to execute a sale deed free from encumbrances.
The buyer did not pay or indicate willingness to pay the balance by the contractual deadline and produced no timely communication asking the sellers to clear the mortgage or complete the sale.

The buyer’s first demand for performance came in response to the sellers’ notice rescinding the contract; the buyer first sought an injunction against alienation and filed the specific-performance suit about three years after the contractual deadline.
The buyer relied on bank passbooks for accounts opened after the contractual period and did not produce evidence that he had funds to pay the balance during that period.
The trial court did not frame an issue on readiness and willingness and relied on the buyer’s asserted means without adequately examining his conduct or the contract terms.
issues.conclusion: The buyer failed to prove that he had continuously been ready and willing to perform the contract, so he was not entitled to specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires the plaintiff to plead and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform essential contractual terms; the plaintiff bears the burden, and actual tender or deposit is generally unnecessary unless directed by the court. Readiness concerns financial capacity, while willingness is assessed from conduct and surrounding circumstances. The court relied on JP Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao, His Holiness Acharya Swami Ganesh Dassji v. Sita Ram Thapar, Atma Ram v. Charanjit Singh, and P. Meenakshisundaram v. P. Vijayakumar.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and contract_made_balance_payment_precede_sale_deed and buyer_did_not_offer_balance_by_deadline and buyer_did_not_urge_seller_to_complete_in_time and buyer_lacked_contemporaneous_proof_of_funds and buyer_delayed_specific_performance_action

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The buyer brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.contract_made_balance_payment_precede_sa: The agreement required the buyer to pay the balance before the seller had to execute the sale deed free of encumbrances.
predicates.buyer_did_not_offer_balance_by_deadline: The buyer neither paid nor indicated willingness to pay the balance by the time fixed for performance.
predicates.buyer_did_not_urge_seller_to_complete_in: The buyer did not timely communicate with the seller to request completion of the sale or clearance of the encumbrance.
predicates.buyer_lacked_contemporaneous_proof_of_fu: The buyer produced no evidence showing financial capacity to pay the balance during the contractual period.
predicates.buyer_delayed_specific_performance_actio: The buyer sought an injunction against alienation before later bringing a specific-performance claim, and did not bring that claim until well after the contractual deadline.

issues.definition: When a buyer seeks specific performance but the agreement requires balance payment before conveyance and the buyer neither timely offers payment nor urges completion, lacks contemporaneous proof of funds, and delays the specific-performance claim, readiness and willingness are not proven.

issues.legal_issue: The discretionary remedy of specific performance may be refused where the claimant’s conduct and the circumstances of the transaction make enforcement inequitable, even when time and increased property value are considered.
material_facts: The buyer’s conduct showed prolonged inaction and a lack of demonstrated willingness to complete the transaction.
Several decades had passed since the agreement, during which the property’s value had undoubtedly increased.
The buyer had withdrawn the balance consideration deposited in court.
The court considered the buyer’s conduct in deciding whether to grant specific performance and ordered return of the advance with interest instead.
issues.conclusion: The court declined to grant specific performance and directed that the advance be refunded with interest.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 confers discretion to grant specific performance, which must be exercised on sound, reasonable, and equitable principles. Delay and price escalation alone do not justify refusal; the court considers the totality of circumstances, including the parties’ conduct, responsibility for delay, unfair advantage, and hardship. The court relied on Zarina Siddiqui v. A. Ramalingam, Satya Jain v. Anis Ahmed Rushdie, Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P.) Ltd., and K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and buyer_conduct_inconsistent_with_completion and long_lapse_since_agreement and property_value_rose_substantially

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The buyer brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.buyer_conduct_inconsistent_with_completi: The buyer did not timely pursue completion, delayed bringing the specific-performance claim, and later withdrew the balance deposited in court.
predicates.long_lapse_since_agreement: A substantial period passed between the agreement and the court’s decision on specific performance.
predicates.property_value_rose_substantially: The value of the property increased substantially during the period of delay and litigation.

issues.definition: When a buyer seeks specific performance but has acted inconsistently with completing the sale, a substantial period has passed, and the property has substantially increased in value, the court may refuse specific performance and order the advance refunded.
